strengths: The paper addresses a critical problem in vision-based robot navigation: achieving agile, safe, and omnidirectional continuous control from surround-view RGB cameras in tight, cluttered, and dynamic scenes.

The proposed multi-teacher distillation framework is well-designed. Training specialized RL experts with privileged depth information across specific navigation modes (reaching, squeezing, dynamic avoiding) and distilling them into a unified VLA policy via capability-balanced DAgger iterations is effective and principled.

Comprehensive simulation experiments in IsaacLab across multiple challenging environments demonstrate clear improvements in success rate and weighted travel time over prior learning-based planners (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP).

The physical system is successfully deployed on a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot, showing zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and navigating challenging scenarios such as thin wires/rods and narrow clearances (<1-2 cm).
weaknesses: Fairness of baseline comparisons: The baselines compared in Table I (NavDP, ViPlanner, iPlanner) are fundamentally single-camera (front-facing) systems, whereas MM-Nav uses a 4-camera 360-degree surround view. While the authors mention field-of-view as a limitation of baselines, it is difficult to decouple how much gain stems from the multi-view sensor setup versus the VLA architecture and multi-expert training. A baseline equipped with multi-view inputs or a single-view ablation of MM-Nav would strengthen the claims.

Lack of quantitative real-world evaluation: Real-world results are presented almost exclusively qualitatively via images and narrative descriptions. Reporting quantitative metrics (e.g., success rates, collision rates, number of interventions over N trials) in the physical testbeds would make the sim-to-real transfer claims much more convincing.

State estimation details in deployment: For real-world navigation, the goal $g_t$ is supplied as a relative coordinate. The paper lacks details on how real-world localization/odometry is tracked on the robot to compute $g_t$ over time, and how sensitive the policy is to odometry drift.

System latency and networking: Deploying a 7B VLA model on a remote RTX 5090 server introduces network communication and round-trip latency. A brief discussion or latency breakdown regarding its impact on agile collision avoidance with dynamic obstacles (moving at up to 1.5 m/s) would be valuable.

strengths: Compelling framework bridging privileged RL expert training and multi-view VLA policy learning: Distilling specialized depth-based RL experts (reaching, squeezing, avoiding) into a unified surround-view (360°) RGB-only VLA student is well-motivated and executed.

Effective capability-balanced data aggregation: The proposed DAgger-style iteration with dynamically weighted data sampling (based on the Weighted Travel Time performance gap) is sound and demonstrably accelerates convergence while preventing catastrophic forgetting of individual capabilities.

Continuous control at competitive inference speed: Unlike many prior navigation VLAs restricted to discrete primitive actions, MM-Nav outputs continuous omnidirectional velocities (v_x, v_y, v_yaw) and runs at ~7 Hz using tiered visual tokenization.

Comprehensive simulation evaluation and ablations: Experiments in IsaacLab validate the synergistic benefits of multi-expert learning (Table II) and the necessity of balanced aggregation (Fig. 6) over single-expert policies and unified RL baselines.

Physical robot deployment: Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated on a Unitree Go2 quadruped in challenging scenarios, including handling thin obstacles, transparent surfaces, and dynamic human intrusions.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison regarding field-of-view: Baselines in Table I (NavDP, ViPlanner, iPlanner) utilize single front-facing camera inputs. Because navigation in squeezing and dynamic avoiding heavily relies on peripheral/rear vision, it is difficult to isolate whether performance gains stem from the multi-expert VLA formulation or simply having 360° visual coverage. Comparing against a multi-view adapted version of NavDP or an equivalent small imitation learning baseline would clarify this.

Lack of quantitative real-world evaluation: Section IV.C and Figure 5 provide compelling qualitative real-world demonstrations, but no quantitative results (e.g., success rate, collision count over multiple trials, or quantitative comparisons against the robot's default navigation stack / baselines) are reported in the physical domain.

Questionable necessity of a 7B LLM for point-goal navigation: The robot receives simple numerical point-goal prompts (e.g., 'Go to the position of <x:10.00, y:0.00>'). While the authors mention co-training with VQA data to reduce the sim-to-real gap, there is no ablation comparing the 7B VLA against a smaller backbone (e.g., a lightweight multi-view ResNet/Transformer policy) to substantiate whether the heavy LLM backbone is truly required.

Offboard inference latency and communication dependency: Running the 7B model requires an offboard server equipped with a high-end RTX 5090 GPU over Wi-Fi. The paper does not thoroughly discuss the impact of network packet loss, latency fluctuations, or sudden disconnections on high-speed continuous velocity control.

strengths: The multi-expert teacher-student framework effectively decomposes navigation into specialized competencies (reaching, squeezing, and avoiding dynamic obstacles) trained with privileged depth simulation, before distilling them into an RGB-based student policy.

Comprehensive simulation results show that multi-expert distillation outperforms both individual single-skill RL policies and a monolithically trained mixed RL expert (Table II), demonstrating skill synergy.
The surround-view (360-degree, 4-camera) setup with continuous velocity control provides superior situational awareness compared to standard discrete single-camera navigation agents.
Physical deployment is demonstrated on a real Unitree Go2 quadruped robot in challenging configurations, such as narrow passages and thin obstacles.
weaknesses: Confounded baseline comparisons: Baselines such as NavDP, ViPlanner, and iPlanner only use a single front-facing camera, whereas the proposed method utilizes a 4-camera 360-degree surround-view system. As acknowledged in Section IV.B, the primary failure mode of the baselines is limited FOV. To isolate the contribution of the multi-expert VLA distillation architecture, the authors must compare against multi-camera versions of standard navigation baselines (e.g., multi-view NavDP or multi-view BC/RL).

Lack of quantitative real-world evaluation: Real-world results are purely anecdotal and qualitative (Fig. 1 and Fig. 5). The paper does not report any quantitative real-world metrics (e.g., success rate over N trials, collision counts, traversal speed, or comparative trials against baselines) in any of the four test environments.

Architectural overhead for point-goal navigation: Deploying a 7B-parameter vision-language model (requiring an off-board RTX 5090 GPU to reach 7 Hz) solely to predict continuous (vx, vy, vyaw) velocities toward a numerical (x, y) coordinate is computationally excessive. The paper does not adequately justify why an LLM/VLA backbone is required over standard lightweight visual-motor policies trained on surround-view RGB images.

Missing ablation on open-world VQA co-training: The authors claim that co-training with open-world VQA data bridges the sim-to-real gap, yet no ablation experiment is provided to demonstrate the necessity or quantitative effect of this auxiliary loss on either simulation or real-world performance.

Drafting, formatting, and reference inconsistencies: The manuscript uses an IEEE conference template rather than standard ECCV formatting, contains an empty placeholder for the project page URL on Page 1, and exhibits figure reference confusion (e.g., Page 5 references Fig. 6 prematurely before discussing Fig. 4).

strengths: Comprehensive and well-engineered system pipeline that effectively addresses continuous omnidirectional visual navigation using a 360-degree multi-view Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture.

The multi-expert distillation paradigm with capability-balanced online DAgger refinement is sound and intuitively addresses the skill-imbalance problem across diverse behaviors (reaching, squeezing, dynamic avoiding).

Strong empirical results on the standard InternVLA-N1 System-1 benchmark, substantially outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods (e.g., NavDP, InternVLA-N1) in both single-view and multi-view setups.

Convincing ablation studies, particularly highlighting the role of real-world VQA co-training in bridging the sim-to-real gap, supported by latent representation alignment analysis (UMAP/gap-axis projection).

Real-world physical robotic deployment on a Unitree Go2 quadruped across difficult corner cases (such as thin wire avoidance, transparent glass walls, and moving pedestrians) at a practical control frequency (~7 Hz).
weaknesses: Language utilization in the VLA framework is relatively shallow for navigation itself; the text prompt primarily acts as a numerical goal coordinate container ('Go to the position of <x, y>') rather than leveraging rich semantic instruction following.

Real-world evaluations lack quantitative comparisons against alternative navigation baselines (e.g., comparing directly against baseline visual navigation policies on physical hardware rather than only comparing with/without VQA ablations).

Inference relies on an off-board server equipped with a high-end RTX 5090 GPU over network transmission rather than edge computation, which may introduce latency and safety considerations in practical field deployments.

strengths: Well-motivated hybrid framework that systematically tackles data scarcity and hazardous scenario training by training capability-specific RL experts with privileged depth in simulation and distilling them into a visual-only VLA student.

The capability-balanced iterative refinement strategy dynamically adapts the data distribution across reaching, squeezing, and avoiding based on weighted travel time gaps, mitigating capability imbalance during DAgger-style fine-tuning.

Thoughtful architectural design combining tiered visual token compression (fine-grained current frame tokens, coarse history tokens) with continuous omnidirectional velocity output, allowing a 7B model to run at 7 Hz inference speed with 360-degree observation.

Co-training on real-world VQA data is thoroughly analyzed both quantitatively and qualitatively, including informative UMAP/gap-axis latent feature visualizations demonstrating how VQA data bridges the sim-to-real representation shift.

Strong experimental evaluation on both a public benchmark (InternVLA-N1 S1, where it surpasses prior methods by a notable margin) and custom IsaacLab environments, complemented by zero-shot real-world physical deployment on a quadruped robot across challenging scenarios (e.g., thin wires, dynamic pedestrian avoidance).
weaknesses: Task formulation remains restricted to point-goal navigation (conditioned merely on coordinate prompts). Given the high capacity of a 7B LLM backbone, the paper does not assess whether the language capabilities can be leveraged for open-vocabulary semantic goals or natural language instruction following (VLN/ObjectNav).

Real-world deployment relies on offloading inference to an external high-end workstation (NVIDIA RTX 5090) over wireless transmission. The paper lacks discussion on wireless latency, network instability, and the feasibility of on-device execution.

Real-world physical experiments compare only the proposed method with and without VQA data over 20 trials per scenario; comparisons against other standard real-world visual navigation baselines in the physical setting are missing.

strengths: Well-motivated capability-decoupled distillation framework: Decomposing visual navigation into distinct specialized skills (reaching, squeezing, dynamic obstacle avoidance) trained via privileged RL teachers, and distilling them into a unified VLA policy effectively circumvents the training instability of monolithic RL agents.

Capability-balanced iterative refinement: The proposed dynamic data aggregation scheme, guided by performance gaps (Weighted Travel Time), systematically prevents catastrophic forgetting and addresses skill imbalance across training iterations.

Comprehensive empirical validation: MM-Nav demonstrates notable gains on the InternVLA-N1 benchmark over prior RGB-D and depth-based baselines while operating purely on RGB inputs, along with thorough ablations on VQA co-training, camera views, and iteration dynamics.

Real-world deployment and engineering execution: Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree GO2 platform across challenging conditions (thin wires, moving pedestrians, night-time alleys), operating at ~7 Hz via an efficient tiered visual tokenization architecture.
weaknesses: Narrow instruction formulation for a VLA architecture: Although a 7B VLA foundation model is used, the navigation task is formulated essentially as point-goal navigation with numerical coordinate prompts rather than open-ended visual-language semantic navigation (e.g., ObjectNav or VLN instructions), leaving the high-level semantic capabilities of the LLM backbone somewhat underutilized.

Off-board compute dependency: Deployment requires streaming camera feeds to an off-board server equipped with high-end workstation hardware (NVIDIA RTX 5090) to achieve 7 Hz control, posing bandwidth, latency, and operational constraints for untethered real-world applications.

Limited depth-to-RGB distillation analysis: The privileged RL teachers operate on depth while the student policy operates purely on surround-view RGB. While latent space visualizations (UMAP) illustrate sim-to-real domain alignment via VQA data, deeper analysis into how implicit geometric depth cues are learned from multi-view RGB without direct depth auxiliary supervision is limited.
